title: If We Had Played at 50 Per Cent Against Australia, We Would Have Made the Semis: Savita Punia and Salima Tete on India's World Cup Campaign
excerpt: In exclusive interviews after India's best Women's Hockey World Cup finish in 52 years, the captain and veteran goalkeeper reflect on near-misses, the Marijne effect and Asian Games ambitions
body:
• Captain Salima Tete and goalkeeper Savita Punia spoke exclusively to NDTV and RevSportz after India's best Women's Hockey World Cup finish in 52 years
  • Punia called the quarterfinal loss to Australia a painful "what if," saying the team played at far below their level in that match
  • Both players credited coach Sjoerd Marijne's six-month transformation — rebuilding unity, fitness and tactical awareness — for the turnaround
  • Tete said the Asian Games preparation will focus on penalty corner attack, possession and end-phase composure, with LA 2028 Olympic qualification the ultimate target
  • Punia revealed she may step away after the Asian Games but expressed full confidence in Bichu Devi Kharibam as her successor between the posts

Hours after India sealed a fifth-place finish at the 2026 Women's Hockey World Cup in Amstelveen — their best result at the tournament since 1974 — captain Salima Tete and veteran goalkeeper Savita Punia sat down for exclusive interviews with NDTV and RevSportz. The tone was one of quiet pride mixed with lingering regret: the team knew they could have gone further.

The Australia Match Still Hurts

India's campaign ended at the quarterfinal stage with a loss to Australia, and Punia was candid about what that meant. "Even while I was in the goal, I was thinking that if we had played at 50 per cent of our level against Australia, maybe we would have played the semi-final," she told NDTV's Rica Roy. "It's not that Australia played exceptionally well."

https://x.com/Sports_NDTV/status/2093342212319047926

Speaking separately to RevSportz, Punia added broader context. "We knew we could have done better. Despite the doubts surrounding us, especially after previous defeats to China, we focused on ourselves, trusted our coaches and believed in our abilities," she said. She also recalled a telling moment: Dutch drag-flicker Yibbi Jansen, one of the world's best, said "it is not easy to play against India."

"Our body language, confidence and the way opponents perceive us have changed a lot. We want to finish on the podium, and I believe that day is not far away."

— Savita Punia, India goalkeeper

Eleven Debutants, One Historic Result

The achievement is remarkable in context. Punia noted that 11 of the 20 players in the squad were making their World Cup debut. "Without experience, you can't achieve anything quickly," she said. "But the new players, especially the young players, performed beyond what we demanded of them."

Tete, who captained the side, spoke about the role her senior teammates played in keeping her motivated. "Bichchu [Devi] and Savita always say, 'We need you.' That always motivates me," she told NDTV. "Even the junior players say, 'Sister, you have to play more.' If I play, the team will do better."

The Marijne Effect

Both players pointed to the return of Dutch coach Sjoerd Marijne as the catalyst for India's resurgence. Marijne, who coached India to a fourth-place finish at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, came back to a team that had missed the Paris Olympics and been relegated from the Pro League.

"When he came, he came with a good vision. He didn't hurry at all. First, we worked on our fitness," Punia said. She described how Marijne prioritized team bonding — giving players unity bands and crystals — alongside tactical work on defence, penalty corners and attack. "We believe in each other because he believes in us."

In a lighter moment, Punia revealed that Marijne has picked up some Hindi during his four years with the team. "He says everything in English, but in the end, he says, 'Samajh gaye?'"

Tete praised Marijne's direct communication style. "Our coach directly tells us, 'I need this from you,'" she said. "Even after we make a mistake, he gives us instructions. There is no gap in communication."

The Goalkeeper Bond

One of the more striking revelations was the relationship between Punia and backup goalkeeper Bichu Devi Kharibam. Despite being competitors for the same position, Punia described their bond as a source of strength. "Very few goalkeepers have such a relationship," she said. "It doesn't matter to us whether I start or Bichchu starts."

In her RevSportz interview, Punia was open about the future. "If I decide to step away afterwards, I can do so happily knowing that Bichu is ready to take over and do a great job for the team," she said. Punia has won two bronze medals and a silver at the Asian Games — a gold would complete the set.

Eyes on the Asian Games and LA 2028

With the Asian Games scheduled for next month, both players are already looking ahead. Tete outlined specific areas the team will target during training in Bangalore: penalty corner attack, ball possession and end-phase composure.

Punia was careful not to single out China as the only threat, despite them being the expected main rival. "This is my fourth Asian Games. No medal was easy. We had to fight for every medal," she said. "You can't take any match easy."

The bigger prize is LA 2028 Olympic qualification, which would come through a strong Asian Games result. "Given how much we have improved under Sjoerd in six months, I believe we can get very close to the Olympic podium, with a year and a half of preparation before LA," Punia said.

"The future of Indian women's hockey is very bright because we are now on the right track."

— Savita Punia
